Recommendation
For best practical performance, you should choose std::sort. Although theoretical analysis suggests that randomized QuickSort handles uniformly distributed data efficiently, the Standard Library implementation is exceptionally optimized for real-world scenarios. std::sort typically employs Introsort, a hybrid algorithm that combines QuickSort, HeapSort, and InsertionSort. This design guarantees O(n log n) time complexity while avoiding the worst-case O(n^2) pitfalls of pure QuickSort. For 10^7 doubles, the low constant factors, branch prediction optimizations, and cache-friendly behavior provided by highly tuned vendor implementations (like libstdc++ or MSVC STL) will almost certainly outperform a manual, home-brewed QuickSort, even if that custom code assumes favorable data distribution.

Supporting basis
Empirical benchmarks on modern hardware consistently show std::sort outperforming naive custom QuickSort. On an array of 10^7 uniform doubles, std::sort typically achieves ~0.4–0.6 seconds, leveraging SIMD instructions and optimized recursion limits. A custom recursive QuickSort often lags at ~0.8–1.2 seconds due to suboptimal pivot selection, stack overhead, and lack of compiler-specific intrinsics. Furthermore, std::sort protects against pathological inputs that could truncate the entire 10-million-element array into quadratic time, jeopardizing latency reliability. The standard library benefits from decades of low-level optimization, including tree-partitioning and iterative depth handling. While a custom algorithm might theoretically save one recursive call layer, the cumulative gains from inlining, loop unrolling, and memory access patterns in the standard implementation provide a decisive, measurable performance advantage in controlled, uniform-distribution scenarios.<|im_end|>
